welcome.text: Welcome. Sit tall, or lie down. Let your eyes close, and let the day go quiet for a few minutes.

nose.text: Breathe only through your nose. It warms and filters the air, and it's where your sinuses add nitric oxide to every breath.

ribs.text: Let the ribs widen to the sides, like a band stretching. Shoulders still, belly soft. Breathe in with no more effort than at rest.

ladder_intro.text: Now we'll lengthen the breath, step by step. Follow the circle.

ladder_up2.text: And longer still. Smooth and even.

hum_intro.text: Humming breath. Breathe in through the nose, then hum the whole exhale, lips closed, jaw soft. Let the sound fill your head.

hum_science.text: Humming makes the air in your sinuses vibrate. In studies, it raised nitric oxide in the nose about fifteen-fold. In the lab, nitric oxide slows cold viruses.

hum_space.text: The first hum gives the biggest boost, so we'll hum again at the end, once your sinuses have refilled.

r1_intro.text: Round one. Kapalabhati. Short, sharp exhales through the nose, pulled from the belly. The inhale takes care of itself. Keep your face soft.

r2_intro.text: Round two. A few more breaths this time. Same easy rhythm.

r3_intro.text: Last round. Let this be the easiest one.

g_intro.text: Slow, full breaths through the nose. Then a soft hold, with empty lungs.

r1_tingle.text: Tingling or lightness is normal. The fast breathing lowered your carbon dioxide, and rising carbon dioxide is what makes you want to breathe. It's a signal, not an emergency.

r2_hunger.text: Air hunger is just a sensation. Notice it without arguing with it. Soften your jaw, your eyes, your hands.

r3_still.text: Nothing to do. Just the stillness of an empty breath.

inhale_top.text: Breathe in. Fill all the way to the top, and hold.

bandha.text: Gently lift the pelvic floor, and bring the chin slightly down. Hold the breath as if it's resting, not trapped.

bandha_short.text: Root lock. Chin down. Stay soft.

full_science.text: With full lungs, oxygen stays high while carbon dioxide slowly rises. That's where your tolerance is built.

release.text: And let it go. Breathe naturally.

kox.text: In a 2014 study, people trained in this kind of breathing released a surge of adrenaline, and their inflammatory response to a bacterial toxin was roughly halved. Not a cold. But a sign your breath can talk to your immune system.

cool_intro.text: Now cool down. In for four, out for eight. Slow and quiet.

cool_science.text: A long exhale turns up the vagus nerve, your body's brake pedal. Less stress is one of the few things linked to catching fewer colds.

hum_again.text: Three last hums. Long and low.

checkin.text: Let the breath go. Notice how you feel. Warmth, quiet, whatever is here.

close.text: That's your practice. Keep warm, have something hot to drink, and get to bed early. If a fever comes, rest instead, or choose the gentle version.
